# Oregon Drug Help — full text

> Free, plain-language help for drug and alcohol use in Oregon.

# Oregon Drug Help: Free Drug & Alcohol Help in Oregon
URL: https://oregondrughelp.com/
Last reviewed: 2026-11-03

Free help anywhere in Oregon

# You don’t have to figure this out alone.
Clear, kind information about drugs, alcohol, treatment and recovery in Oregon, for you or for someone you love. No judgment, no jargon.
Talk to someone today Find where to start

## Need help with drugs or alcohol in Oregon? Start here.
- Talk to someone now: call the Oregon Alcohol & Drug Helpline at 1-800-923-4357. It’s free, confidential and open 24/7.
- Pay nothing for treatment: the Oregon Health Plan (OHP) covers detox, medication, outpatient and residential treatment at no cost to members. How to get free treatment
- Overdose: call 911 and give naloxone (Narcan). Oregon law protects people who call for help from drug possession charges. What to do
- Local help: every Oregon county has a Behavioral Health Resource Network with screening, peer support and treatment. Find yours

## Where are you today?
Pick the one that feels closest. You can change your mind at any point.

### I’m worried about my own use
A free, confidential call to the Oregon Alcohol & Drug Helpline is a good first step. They listen, and they can point you to treatment near you. See who to call

### I’m worried about someone I love
Find words that open the door, ways to keep them safer, and support for you too. Read the family guide

### I’m worried about overdose
How to spot an overdose, how to use naloxone, and where to get it in Oregon. Learn what to do

### I can’t afford treatment
How the Oregon Health Plan covers treatment at no cost, and what to do if you have no insurance. Find free treatment

## Reaching out is the hardest part, and you’ve already started.
These lines are free and confidential. You don’t need to be sure about anything before you call.
1-800-923-4357Oregon Alcohol & Drug HelplineRun by Lines for Life. Support and treatment referrals, 24/7. 988988 Suicide & Crisis LifelineCall or text any time, for any kind of crisis, including drug or alcohol use. 211211infoCall 211 to find local services across Oregon: treatment, housing, food and more. 1-877-968-8491YouthLineFor teens and young adults. Or text teen2teen to 839863.

## What help can look like
There’s no single route. Most people use a mix of these over time.

Medical detox
Supervised care to get through withdrawal safely. Withdrawal from alcohol and some drugs can be dangerous on your own.

Medication
Prescribed treatments like buprenorphine and methadone that ease cravings and withdrawal for opioids, plus options for alcohol.

Therapy and counseling
One-on-one or group sessions that build skills for cravings, stress and relationships.

Outpatient care
Treatment that fits around work, school and family, with regular visits.

Residential programs
Stay somewhere safe and structured for a few weeks or months while you focus on recovery.

Peer support
Peer mentors and groups led by people who’ve been there, in person or online.

## When it’s someone you love
You can’t make someone change, but how you show up makes a real difference.

### Start with care, not blame
Pick a calm, sober moment. Say what you’ve seen and how you feel: “I’ve noticed you seem exhausted, and I’m worried about you.”

### Keep them safer
Keep naloxone at home and learn how to use it. Ask them not to use alone. Staying alive comes first.

### Look after yourself
Family support groups, counseling and helplines are there for you too. Call 1-800-923-4357 even if your loved one isn’t ready.

## Find treatment and services
Trusted, free places to search for care in Oregon.
- Lines for Life: Alcohol & Drug HelplineTalk with someone 24/7 about options for you or a loved one. (https://www.linesforlife.org/our-lines/alcohol-and-drug-helpline/)
- 211infoSearch local treatment, housing, food and health services across Oregon. (https://www.211info.org/)
- FindTreatment.govFederal search tool for licensed treatment programs by location and type of care. (https://findtreatment.gov/)
- Help in your countyBehavioral Health Resource Networks and county behavioral health programs.
- YouthLinePeer support for teens and young adults by call, text or chat. (https://oregonyouthline.org/)

## Common questions

Who do I call for drug or alcohol help in Oregon?
Call the Oregon Alcohol & Drug Helpline at 1-800-923-4357. It’s free, confidential and open 24/7, run by the nonprofit Lines for Life. They can talk through what’s happening and refer you to treatment near you. If it’s a crisis, call or text 988. If someone isn’t breathing, call 911.
Is drug treatment free in Oregon?
It can be. The Oregon Health Plan (OHP) covers drug and alcohol treatment at no cost to members, including detox, medication, outpatient and residential care. If you don’t have insurance, you can apply for OHP any time at 800-699-9075. See our free treatment guide.
What should I do if someone is overdosing?
Call 911, give naloxone (Narcan) if you have it, support their breathing and stay with them. Oregon’s Good Samaritan law protects people who call for help from drug possession charges. See what to do in an overdose.
Can I get help for a family member who won’t go to treatment?
Yes. You can call 1-800-923-4357 even if your loved one isn’t ready. Keep naloxone at home, ask them not to use alone, and look after your own wellbeing with support groups or counseling.

## Sources

# Free and Low-Cost Drug Treatment in Oregon
URL: https://oregondrughelp.com/free-treatment/
Last reviewed: 2026-11-03

-
-

# Free and low-cost drug and alcohol treatment in Oregon
How to get treatment paid for through the Oregon Health Plan, private insurance or Medicare, and where to turn if you have no insurance at all.
Last reviewed November 3, 2026 · Sources listed at the bottom of this page

## The short answer
- On the Oregon Health Plan (OHP), treatment is free. OHP covers detox, medication, counseling, outpatient and residential treatment at no cost to members.
- Apply for OHP any time at 800-699-9075 (Monday to Friday, 7 a.m. to 6 p.m.) or at oregonhealthplan.gov.
- No referral needed: OHP members can usually start substance use treatment without seeing their regular doctor first.
- No insurance? Call 1-800-923-4357 for free referrals to programs that serve uninsured people, and ask about sliding-scale fees.

## The Oregon Health Plan pays for treatment
The Oregon Health Plan (OHP) is Oregon’s Medicaid program. If you’re a member, drug and alcohol treatment costs you nothing. OHP covers:
- Withdrawal management (detox), with medical supervision
- Medication for opioid use disorder, including methadone and buprenorphine (Suboxone)
- Counseling and therapy, one-on-one or in groups
- Outpatient and intensive outpatient programs
- Residential treatment, where you live at the program for a time
You can usually start substance use treatment without a referral from your doctor. Some services, like residential treatment, may need approval from your OHP plan first. The program you choose can usually handle that for you.

## How to apply for OHP

| How | Details
| By phone | 800-699-9075
| Hours | Monday to Friday, 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. Pacific
| Online | oregonhealthplan.gov (https://www.oregonhealthplan.gov/)
| In person | Local community partner organizations help with applications for free
| When | Any time of year. There’s no enrollment period.
Already on OHP? Call the member services number on your OHP card and say you’re looking for substance use treatment. They’ll help you find a provider in your plan.

## If you have private insurance or Medicare
Most private health plans and Medicare cover addiction treatment. Call the number on your insurance card and ask about your substance use disorder benefits: which programs are in network, what you’ll pay, and whether you need approval first.

## If you have no insurance
- Apply for OHP. Many people who think they won’t qualify do, especially if their income has dropped.
- Call for a referral. The Oregon Alcohol & Drug Helpline (1-800-923-4357) and SAMHSA’s National Helpline (1-800-662-4357) can point you to programs that serve uninsured people, and both are free.
- Contact your county’s Behavioral Health Resource Network. Every Oregon county has one. They bill insurance when you have it, and can connect you to services when you don’t. Find yours.
- Ask about sliding-scale fees. Many treatment programs lower their prices based on income. FindTreatment.gov (https://findtreatment.gov/) lets you search for them.

## Common questions

Is drug rehab free in Oregon?
For Oregon Health Plan (OHP) members, yes. OHP covers substance use treatment at no cost, including detox, medication, outpatient care and residential treatment. Without OHP, cost depends on your insurance, but many programs offer sliding-scale fees.
Does the Oregon Health Plan cover rehab?
Yes. OHP covers withdrawal management (detox), medication such as methadone and buprenorphine, counseling, outpatient programs and residential treatment. Some services, especially residential care, may need approval from your OHP plan first.
Do I need a referral to get treatment on OHP?
Usually not. OHP members can generally start mental health or substance use treatment without a referral from their primary care provider. Call the member services number on your OHP card to find a provider.
How do I apply for the Oregon Health Plan?
Call 800-699-9075 (Monday to Friday, 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. Pacific) or apply online through oregonhealthplan.gov. You can apply at any time of year, and local community partners can help you fill out the application for free.
Can I get drug treatment in Oregon without insurance?
Yes. Apply for OHP first, since many people qualify. Meanwhile, call the Oregon Alcohol & Drug Helpline at 1-800-923-4357 or SAMHSA at 1-800-662-4357 for referrals to programs that serve uninsured people, and contact your county’s Behavioral Health Resource Network.

## Sources
Last reviewed November 3, 2026. Services and phone numbers can change, so check with each provider.
- Oregon Health Authority: Contact the Oregon Health Plan (https://www.oregon.gov/OHA/HSD/OHP/Pages/Contact-Us.aspx)
- CareOregon: Mental health and substance use treatment (https://careoregon.org/members/mental-health-and-substance-use-treatment)
- Health Share of Oregon: Mental health and substance use benefits (https://www.healthshareoregon.org/members/my-health-plan/mental-health-substance-use)
- Health Share of Oregon: Apply for OHP (https://healthshareoregon.org/members/enroll-or-renew)
- Oregon Health Authority: Behavioral Health Resource Networks (https://www.oregon.gov/oha/BH/Adults/Pages/BHRN.aspx)
- FindTreatment.gov (SAMHSA) (https://findtreatment.gov/)
- SAMHSA National Helpline (https://www.samhsa.gov/find-help/helplines/national-helpline)

# Find Drug and Alcohol Help in Your Oregon County
URL: https://oregondrughelp.com/find-help-by-county/
Last reviewed: 2026-11-03

-
-

# Find drug and alcohol help in your Oregon county
Every county in Oregon has a Behavioral Health Resource Network: local agencies that offer screening, peer support, harm reduction and treatment. Here’s how to reach yours.
Last reviewed November 3, 2026 · Sources listed at the bottom of this page

## The short answer
- Every Oregon county or Tribal area has at least one Behavioral Health Resource Network (BHRN) for people with substance use disorders or harmful substance use.
- BHRNs offer screening and referral, a personal plan, low-barrier treatment, harm reduction, peer support and help finding work.
- To find yours: use the state’s BHRN directory (https://www.oregon.gov/oha/BH/Providers/Documents/BHRN-Directory.pdf) (sorted by county), dial 211, or call 1-800-923-4357.

## What a BHRN can help with
Behavioral Health Resource Networks were set up in 2021 so that anyone struggling with drugs or alcohol has somewhere local to go. Each network is a group of agencies in your county that work together. You can walk in, call, or be referred by someone else.
- Screening and referral: a conversation about what’s going on and what kind of help fits
- A personal plan built with you, not for you
- Low-barrier treatment that’s easy to start
- Harm reduction, such as naloxone and safer-use supplies
- Peer support from people with their own recovery experience
- Employment support to help you get or keep work

### Three ways to find your county’s network
- Search the state directory. The Oregon Health Authority’s BHRN directory (PDF) (https://www.oregon.gov/oha/BH/Providers/Documents/BHRN-Directory.pdf) lists every agency by county, with phone numbers.
- Dial 211. Ask for the Behavioral Health Resource Network in your county.
- Call 1-800-923-4357. The Oregon Alcohol & Drug Helpline can connect you, 24/7.

## County behavioral health pages
Some counties publish their own guides to local services. We list a county here only once we’ve checked its page.
- Clackamas CountyBehavioral Health Resource Network. Open to anyone living in Clackamas County, with no insurance or referral required. (https://www.clackamas.us/behavioralhealth/network)
- Deschutes CountyCounty Behavioral Health services, including substance use treatment. (https://www.deschutescounty.gov/behavioralhealth)
- Multnomah CountyBehavioral health and substance use services for adults. (https://multco.us/behavioral-health/system-care-adults)
- Washington CountyBehavioral Health Resource Network and partner providers. (https://www.washingtoncountyor.gov/addictions/bhrn)
Your county isn’t listed? Use the state directory (https://www.oregon.gov/oha/BH/Providers/Documents/BHRN-Directory.pdf) or dial 211.

## Common questions

What is a Behavioral Health Resource Network (BHRN)?
A BHRN is a group of local agencies in each Oregon county that work together to serve people with substance use disorders or harmful substance use. They were created by Senate Bill 755 in 2021, which put Measure 110 into practice, and are overseen by the Oregon Health Authority.
What services do BHRNs provide?
Behavioral health screening and referral, individual intervention planning, low-barrier substance use disorder treatment, harm reduction services, peer support, and employment support.
Do I need insurance to use a BHRN?
No insurance is required to reach out. BHRN agencies bill your insurance if you have it, including OHP. If you don’t, ask what they can offer. Some county programs serve people based on ability to pay.
How do I find the BHRN in my county?
Open the Oregon Health Authority’s BHRN directory, which lists agencies by county, or dial 211 and ask for the Behavioral Health Resource Network in your county. The Oregon Alcohol & Drug Helpline (1-800-923-4357) can also connect you.

## Sources

- Clackamas County: Behavioral Health Resource Network (https://www.clackamas.us/behavioralhealth/network)
- Washington County: Behavioral Health Resource Network (https://www.washingtoncountyor.gov/addictions/bhrn)

- Deschutes County: Behavioral Health (https://www.deschutescounty.gov/behavioralhealth)

# Overdose Help: Naloxone and Oregon’s Good Samaritan Law
URL: https://oregondrughelp.com/overdose/
Last reviewed: 2026-11-03

-
-

# What to do if someone is overdosing
Fentanyl is now in much of the drug supply, including fake pills. Knowing the signs and having naloxone on hand saves lives.
Last reviewed November 3, 2026 · Sources listed at the bottom of this page

## In an overdose, do this
- Call 911 right away. Say the person isn’t breathing or won’t wake up, and give your location.
- Give naloxone (Narcan): spray it into one nostril. If there’s no response in 2 to 3 minutes, give another dose.
- Support their breathing with rescue breaths, or roll them onto their side.
- Stay with them until help arrives. Naloxone can wear off before the drugs do.
- You’re protected: Oregon’s Good Samaritan law means you can’t be arrested or prosecuted for drug possession for calling for help.

## Step by step
-
Check for signs. Won’t wake up, slow or no breathing, blue or gray lips or fingertips, gurgling or snoring sounds, tiny pupils.
-
Call 911. Say the person isn’t breathing or won’t wake up, and give your location.
-
Give naloxone (Narcan). Spray it into one nostril. If they don’t respond in 2 to 3 minutes, give another dose.
-
Support their breathing. Give rescue breaths if you know how, or roll them onto their side.
-
Stay with them. Naloxone can wear off before the drugs do, so wait for help to arrive.

### Getting naloxone in Oregon
- Buy it at most pharmacies without a prescription.
- Ask your doctor, clinic or treatment counselor. Many can give it for free.
- Syringe service and harm reduction programs give it out free.
- Your county public health office can tell you where to find free naloxone nearby.
- Your county’s Behavioral Health Resource Network offers harm reduction services, including naloxone.

## Oregon’s Good Samaritan overdose law
Oregon law (ORS 475.898 (https://www.oregonlaws.org/ors/475.898)) is meant to make sure fear of arrest never stops anyone from calling 911. If you call for medical help during an overdose, you and the person overdosing can’t be arrested or prosecuted for:
- Possessing drugs
- Possessing drug paraphernalia
- Being in a place where drugs are used
The law does not protect against other crimes, such as selling drugs, weapons charges or DUI, or against outstanding warrants, including federal warrants and warrants from other states.
This is general information, not legal advice.

## Common questions

Will I get arrested if I call 911 for an overdose in Oregon?
Not for drug possession. Under Oregon’s Good Samaritan overdose law (ORS 475.898), if you call for medical help during an overdose, you and the person overdosing can’t be arrested or prosecuted for possessing drugs or paraphernalia, or for being in a place where drugs are used. The law doesn’t protect against charges like dealing, weapons, DUI, or outstanding warrants.
Do I need a prescription for naloxone in Oregon?
No. Naloxone nasal spray (Narcan) is sold over the counter at pharmacies and many stores without a prescription.
Where can I get free naloxone in Oregon?
Ask your doctor, clinic or treatment counselor, a local syringe service or harm reduction program, or your county public health office. Many give naloxone out for free. If you’re on insurance, a pharmacist can also bill it to your plan.
Can naloxone hurt someone who isn’t overdosing on opioids?
No. Naloxone only works on opioids and won’t harm someone who hasn’t taken them, so if you’re unsure, give it. It can cause sudden withdrawal symptoms in someone who uses opioids regularly.
How long does naloxone last?
Naloxone works for roughly 30 to 90 minutes, which can be shorter than the opioids in someone’s system. That’s why it’s important to call 911 and stay with the person even after they wake up.

## Sources
Last reviewed November 3, 2026. Services and phone numbers can change, so check with each provider.

- Portland Police: Understanding Oregon’s Good Samaritan overdose law (https://www.portland.gov/police/news/2024/9/26/understanding-oregons-good-samaritan-overdose-law-save-lives-without-fear)
- ORS 475.898: Immunity for emergency medical assistance (https://www.oregonlaws.org/ors/475.898)

# About Oregon Drug Help and How We Check Information
URL: https://oregondrughelp.com/about/
Last reviewed: 2026-11-03

-
-

# About Oregon Drug Help
An independent, plain-language guide to getting help with drugs and alcohol in Oregon.
Last reviewed November 3, 2026 · Sources listed at the bottom of this page

## Why this site exists
When you or someone you love is struggling with drugs or alcohol, finding real help is often confusing. Search results are crowded with ads and paid listings for treatment centers. Oregon Drug Help gathers the free, trustworthy options in one place and explains them in plain language.
The site is for anyone in Oregon: people worried about their own use, families and friends, and people in recovery.

## Independent
Oregon Drug Help is not a treatment center and doesn’t refer people to any particular program. We’re not affiliated with any government agency, helpline or provider we mention.

## How we check information
- Official sources first. We rely on the Oregon Health Authority, county health departments, SAMHSA, Oregon law and established nonprofits such as Lines for Life.
- Every page lists its sources at the bottom, so you can check them yourself.
- Every page shows the date it was last reviewed. Phone numbers are checked against the organization’s own website.
- Plain language. We explain medical and legal terms instead of assuming you know them.

## What this site is not
This site gives general information. It isn’t medical or legal advice and can’t replace a conversation with a doctor, counselor or lawyer. If you or someone else is in danger, call 911. In a crisis, call or text 988.

## Sources
Last reviewed November 3, 2026. Services and phone numbers can change, so check with each provider.
- Oregon Health Authority: Substance use (https://www.oregon.gov/oha/bh/adults/pages/substance-use.aspx)
- Lines for Life (https://www.linesforlife.org/)
- SAMHSA: FindTreatment.gov (https://findtreatment.gov/)
